client: I've been really struggling since I started college last semester — I just can't seem to keep up with all the coursework, and it feels like I'm constantly falling behind no matter how hard I try. The worst part is that I've kind of pulled away from the few friends I made at the beginning of the year, because I feel like I don't have time for them, or maybe I'm just embarrassed about how much I'm drowning. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It takes real courage to reach out even when part of you doubts it will help, and I'm genuinely glad you gave it a shot. What you're describing — the pressure of keeping up, the pulling away from friends, that exhausting sense of always being behind — sounds really overwhelming, and it makes complete sense that you're feeling worn down by it all. I'm curious, when you say you feel like you're "drowning," what does that inner voice tend to tell you about *why* that's happening — is it more "college is just this hard for everyone right now," or does it feel more personal, like something is wrong with *you* specifically?

client: Honestly, it feels really personal — like, my brain just keeps telling me that everyone else is figuring it out and I'm the only one who can't get it together. I'll see people in my classes who seem totally fine, turning in assignments on time, and I just think, what is wrong with me that I can't do the same thing? It's hard to shake the feeling that maybe I'm just not smart enough to be here.
therapist: That thought — "maybe I'm just not smart enough to be here" — is such a painful one to carry, and I want you to know it makes sense that your mind went there, even though it's really worth examining how much truth it actually holds. What you're describing, comparing your *inside* experience (the stress, the struggle) to everyone else's *outside* appearance (seeming fine, turning things in), is something almost every college student does, and it's a comparison that's almost always stacked against you. I'm wondering — is there any evidence from your life before college, moments where you *did* figure something out or push through something hard, that might tell a different story than "not smart enough"?

client: I mean, yeah, I did pretty well in high school — I was in honors classes and I actually got a scholarship to come here, so logically I know I'm not completely incompetent. But it's like... that feels like a different lifetime, and part of me wonders if I just got lucky back then, or if high school was just easier and it doesn't really count as proof of anything. I hear what you're saying about the comparison thing, but it's hard to actually believe it when I'm sitting there watching everyone else seem so put together.
therapist: It's really significant that you can hold both of those things at once — the logical knowledge that you earned that scholarship, and the feeling that it somehow "doesn't count" — because that gap between what we *know* and what we *feel* is actually at the heart of what we might want to explore together. That voice that says "it was just luck" is a really common thought pattern where our minds discount evidence that doesn't fit the story we're telling about ourselves, and it's worth noticing how conveniently it dismisses *anything* that might challenge the "not smart enough" narrative. I'm curious — if a close friend came to you with the exact same resume as yours, honors classes, scholarship, and told you "I think I just got lucky," what would you actually say to them?

client: I'd probably tell them that's ridiculous, that you don't get scholarships by luck, and that they should give themselves more credit. But it feels different when it's me — like, I can see the logic for someone else way more easily than I can apply it to myself, and that's kind of frustrating to admit. I guess I see what you're doing with that question, but knowing the double standard exists doesn't automatically make it easier to stop believing the harsher version about myself.
therapist: You're absolutely right, and I want to honor that — insight is a real first step, but it doesn't magically rewire a belief that's probably been reinforced by weeks of stress and exhaustion, so please don't be frustrated with yourself for not being able to just "logic" your way out of it. What actually shifts these deeply held feelings over time is less about knowing the double standard exists and more about gently, repeatedly catching that harsh voice in the moment and practicing responding to yourself with even a fraction of the kindness you'd offer that friend. So I'm wondering — when that "not smart enough" thought shows up most strongly, what's usually happening right before it, is it a specific class, a certain time of day, or something else you've noticed?

client: It's usually late at night when I'm trying to start an assignment and I just kind of freeze — like, I'll sit there staring at the screen and my mind goes blank, and that's when the "you don't belong here" thoughts get really loud. There's also this one calculus class that's been brutal, and every time I get a bad grade back it's like it confirms everything I already feared about myself. I guess I've never really paid attention to the pattern before, but saying it out loud, it does seem like it's tied to specific moments rather than just being constant.
therapist: That's actually a really meaningful observation — noticing that these thoughts spike at specific moments, like late-night freezing or getting a calculus grade back, tells us that they're triggered responses rather than objective truths about who you are, which gives us something concrete to work with. That freezing feeling you describe is often your brain going into a kind of overwhelm mode, where the weight of "I have to prove I belong here" makes even starting feel impossibly high-stakes. I'm curious — when you're sitting there frozen at night, what would feel like the smallest possible step you could take, not to finish the assignment, but just to break that frozen moment, even something almost laughably small?

client: Maybe just opening the document, I guess, or even just writing the date at the top — something that feels so small it's almost stupid. But honestly, my worry is that I'll do that tiny step and then still just sit there frozen, and it'll feel like even that didn't work, which might actually make things worse. I don't know, it's hard to trust that something so small could actually matter when the whole assignment is still looming over me.
therapist: That worry makes a lot of sense, and I don't want to oversell a small step as a magic fix — but I'd gently push back on the idea that it "didn't work" if you write the date and still feel stuck, because just breaking the freeze for even a moment is genuinely different from never starting at all, even if it doesn't feel that way in the moment. The goal of that tiny step isn't to make the whole assignment feel easy, it's just to prove to that frozen part of your brain that you *can* move, which over time starts to quietly chip away at the "I don't belong here" story. I'm wondering — would you be open to trying it just once this week, almost like an experiment rather than a solution, and then noticing what actually happens rather than what you're predicting will happen?

client: I think I can try that — framing it as an experiment rather than something that has to fix everything actually does make it feel a little less loaded. My worry is more about remembering to actually notice what happens instead of just spiraling into the usual thoughts, because in that frozen moment I'm not exactly in a very observant headspace. Maybe I can try it, but I honestly don't know if I'll be able to report back with anything useful.
therapist: That's a really honest and self-aware concern, and it actually points to something worth trying — what if you made the "noticing" part just as small and concrete as the experiment itself, like jotting down one word or a single sentence right after you write that date, just something like "still frozen" or "actually okay" so your observing self has a tiny job it can do even in a hard moment. You don't need to report back with anything polished or useful — even "it felt awful and didn't help" is genuinely valuable information that tells us something real about what you need. And I also just want to say, the fact that you came here skeptical and are leaving willing to try something small is not nothing — so what feels like the most realistic moment this week where you might actually give this a shot?

client: I have a calculus assignment due Thursday, so I'll probably be sitting there frozen sometime Wednesday night — that's honestly the most realistic moment I can think of. I'll try to do the date thing and write one word after, even if that word is just "terrible." I guess I'm a little surprised that this conversation didn't feel as pointless as I expected it to, though I'm still not totally convinced any of this will stick once I'm actually in that moment alone.
therapist: Wednesday night, calculus assignment, one word after the date — that's a real, specific plan, and I want you to hold onto the fact that you built that yourself in this conversation, not me. It's completely okay to still be skeptical, and honestly that one word might *be* "terrible," but you'll have shown yourself that you could move even in a hard moment, and that's the kind of small evidence that slowly starts to rewrite the story your brain tells at midnight. I'd love to hear how Wednesday goes — and in the meantime, I'm curious whether there's one of those friends you've been pulling away from that you might feel even the tiniest bit ready to reach back out to, not to explain everything, but just to reconnect in some small way?

client: There's this one girl, Maya, who I used to eat lunch with at the beginning of the semester, and I've basically gone silent on her for like two months now — so the idea of reaching out feels really awkward, like she's probably just moved on and it would be weird to suddenly reappear. I guess I could send a short text, but I'm honestly more afraid of that than the calculus thing, because if she doesn't respond or seems distant it'll feel like confirmation that I've already messed up those friendships. I don't know, maybe I'm not quite ready for that one yet.
therapist: It's really worth noticing that your brain is doing the exact same thing with Maya that it does with calculus — jumping straight to the worst outcome and treating it as the most likely one, when the reality is that two months isn't that long, and a lot of people are just waiting for someone else to make the first move. And "I'm not quite ready for that one yet" is a completely valid place to be, especially when you've already taken on one experiment this week — you don't have to tackle everything at once. I'm just curious though, if Maya reached out to *you* after two months of silence, what would you actually feel when you saw her name pop up on your phone?

client: Honestly, I'd probably feel really relieved and happy to hear from her — like, I wouldn't think she was weird for reaching out, I'd just be glad she did. I see where you're going with that, and I hate that it makes sense, because it kind of takes away my excuse for not texting her. I still think it feels scarier coming from my side, but I can't really argue that the logic doesn't apply to me the same way it would to her.
therapist: You just did the same thing you did with the scholarship — you caught your own double standard in real time, and that's genuinely hard to do, so give yourself a little credit for that. The fear still being there even when the logic doesn't hold up makes complete sense, because reaching out to Maya feels vulnerable in a way that a calculus document doesn't — it involves another person who could respond in ways you can't control. So I'm not going to push you to text her this week, but I am curious — if you *did* decide she was worth the risk, what's the shortest, lowest-stakes message you could imagine sending her?
